# Results — Study 137 (Mansfield-RS) on real weekly tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py).  Stan Weinstein's Stage-2
filter: buy stocks where price is above a rising 30-week SMA AND Mansfield Relative
Strength (stock / benchmark, each divided by their own 30-week SMA) is positive.
The signal is tested as 13-week forward excess return vs SPY at Stage-2 entries,
compared against a **random-entry control** on the same stocks.  As-of **2026-06-14**.*

*Basket: SPY (benchmark) + 15 large-cap US equities (AAPL MSFT JNJ JPM XOM PG KO WMT
HD BAC PFE CVX MRK ABBV AMZN). Weekly OHLCV from Yahoo Finance, resampled from daily
bars (Friday close).  **Survivorship bias is present** — basket is a current-S&P-500
proxy projected back; positive results should be treated as upper bounds.*

~25 years of weekly data; 30-week SMA warmup leaves ≈ 1,275 usable weeks per ticker.

## The honest test — Stage-2 entry vs random entry (13-week forward excess return)

A Stage-2 entry (transition into Stage 2) is compared against a **matched random-entry
control** on the same stock: the same number of entries, drawn at random weeks after
the SMA warmup period.  The metric is the 13-week forward excess return of the stock
vs SPY (stock gross return minus SPY gross return over the same window).

| Arm | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | skew | HAC *t* |
|-----|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Stage-2 entry** | 811 | **48.1%** | **+29.4** | +0.83 | **+0.72** |
| Random entry (control) | 813 | 49.3% | +118.1 | — | +2.75 |

- The Stage-2 entry signal has a HAC *t* = **+0.72** — **not statistically significant**.
  The signal is indistinguishable from zero after Newey-West correction.
- Stage-2 entries **underperform the random-entry control by −88.7 bps/trade** at 13
  weeks.  The random control is faster, because it enters on any week of a rising stock —
  including the initial surge — while Stage-2 entry waits for the *transition*, which
  often arrives after the best returns have already been collected.
- **Only 2 of 15 stocks** show |*t*| ≥ 2 on the Stage-2 signal (AAPL +3.62, AMZN
  +2.54 — both mega-cap compounders that outperformed across the full 25-year period;
  the rest cluster near zero or negative).  A survivorship-biased basket of current S&P
  winners systematically inflates the stage-2 result for names like AAPL.

The dispersion is wide: 8 of 15 names are negative, only 2 are significantly positive,
and those 2 are names that compounded strongly over the entire 25-year sample regardless
of when you entered them (the survivorship-bias upper bound at work).

## In-Stage-2 holding vs out-of-Stage-2 (next-week excess return)

An alternative question: ignoring *entry* timing, is being inside Stage 2 predictive of
the *next* week's excess return?

| State | n | mean (bps/week) | HAC *t* |
|-------|--:|--:|--:|
| In Stage-2 | 7,423 | +5.7 | +1.61 |
| Out of Stage-2 | 11,534 | +9.2 | +3.04 |

Stocks in Stage 2 earn **5.7 bps/week** excess vs SPY on average (HAC t = 1.61, below
the inference bar), while stocks **out** of Stage 2 earn **9.2 bps/week** (t = 3.04).
The Stage-2 basket does slightly *worse*, not better, than the out-of-stage basket.
The higher out-of-stage mean partly reflects momentum stocks that are about to enter
Stage 2, but the overall picture is that Stage-2 membership is not a strong weekly
predictor of outperformance.

## Hold-period sensitivity (Stage-2 entry vs random-entry control)

| Hold (weeks) | Stage-2 (bps, t) | Random (bps, t) | Delta (bps) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 4  | −6 (+t = −0.37) | +39 (+t = +2.05) | −45 |
| 8  | −31 (t = −1.09) | +87 (t = +2.73) | −118 |
| **13** | **+29 (t = +0.72)** | **+118 (t = +2.75)** | **−89** |
| 26 | +101 (t = +1.26) | +201 (t = +2.73) | −100 |

Across every hold period the Stage-2 entry underperforms the random baseline, with the
random control consistently above the inference bar (*t* > 2) and Stage-2 consistently
below it.

## Tradability

At ~2.2 Stage-2 entries per stock per year (across 15 stocks, ~33 entries/year total)
transaction costs are low in absolute terms, but the gross excess return (+29.4 bps/trade
at 13 weeks) is not statistically significant to begin with:

| Round-trip cost | net mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | +29.4 | +0.72 |
| 1.0 bps | +28.4 | +0.69 |
| 5.0 bps | +24.4 | +0.60 |
| 10.0 bps | +19.4 | +0.47 |

The cost sweep shows the strategy is low-turnover enough that costs don't kill it — but
the underlying gross excess is not significant in the first place.  There is no
"but it works gross" argument; the t-stat never reaches 2.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** HAC *t* = +0.72 on 13-week forward excess return at Stage-2
  entries; far below the inference bar of |*t*| ≥ 2.  Stage-2 entries underperform
  a random-entry control by −88.7 bps/trade across all 15 stocks.  The two stocks with
  |*t*| ≥ 2 are survivorship-biased compounders (AAPL, AMZN) that outperformed under
  any entry timing.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The underlying gross excess is not significant; no level of
  costs can rescue a sub-threshold signal.  The strategy is low-turnover but that
  just means costs don't kill it — the signal was never alive.
- **Timing adds nothing.** Stage-2 entries underperform random entries at every hold
  period tested.  Stocks in Stage 2 earn slightly *less* next-week excess return than
  stocks out of Stage 2.  The filter captures late-trend momentum but misses the initial
  surge — a known feature of any transition-based filter on a trend indicator.
